d9b4a8933d065379: Sahabi Ware / shutterstockA surprising thing has happened at the UN climate conference, Cop31, as it gears up to its conclusion in Antalya, Turkey. Negotiators are discussing how to cool the planet. You might think this should not be surprising, but how to respond to the latest climate science was not on the agenda when the meeting started. Now, the summit’s latest draft decision explicitly recognises a role for carbon dioxide removal (CDR) alongside deep emissions cuts. This is a significant shift, driven by pressure from some of the countries most vulnerable to climate change – the small island states – in response to two alarming scientific reports in the last month. The World Meteorological Organization has confirmed that the rate at which the Earth is heating up is accelerating. One reason is the planet is becoming less “reflective”: the loss of ice and snow, changes in cloud formation and (paradoxically) reductions in atmospheric pollution means that more solar radiation is being absorbed rather than reflected into space. The result is that the Paris Agreement goal of limiting warming to 1.5°C will not be met. There’s a new term for this new warming trajectory: “overshoot”. As a United Nations Environment Programme (Unep) report explains, the best we can hope for now is to exceed 1.5°C but then limit the extent of the overshoot, peaking emissions as soon as possible and then returning to 1.5°C later in the century. Unfortunately, Unep also notes that this may be easier said than done. The longer temperatures remain above 1.5°C, the greater the risk of triggering irreversible changes to systems such as polar ice sheets and glaciers, ocean currents and the Amazon rainforest, which could make returning to lower temperatures impossible. Once a rainforest is lost, it can be extremely difficult to restore – with global climate consequences. finchfocus90 Beyond cutting emissions Up until now we have thought there were basically two responses to global heating. We needed to cut emissions (mitigation), and cope with the warming we experienced (adaptation). But overshoot means that achieving net zero emissions is not enough. By the time we get there the temperature will be too high. Overshoot will require two other kinds of response. As well as cutting the flow of greenhouse gases into the atmosphere, we can physically take them out, a process known as carbon dioxide removal or CDR. And we will also need to consider different ways to increase the planet’s reflectivity. These include limiting aircraft contrails (which trap heat), expanding the white surface areas of the earth (both buildings and crops), or making glaciers more stable. It could potentially include various methods of “solar radiation management”, such as brightening clouds over the oceans, or injecting reflective aerosols into the stratosphere. If any of these “climate cooling” technologies could help bring temperatures down, they need much more carefully governed research. Removing carbon dioxide from the atmosphere is not the same as carbon capture and storage (CCS), which refers to the capture of emissions from industrial plants before they reach the atmosphere. In all net zero scenarios CCS is needed to deal with the residual emissions of fossil fuels. But we now know CDR is going to be required as well – first alongside emissions reduction, to slow warming down, and then to return the global temperature to a safer level. There are various potential removal methods. Some are familiar and uncontroversial, though not yet being done at anything like the required scale. These are natural processes such as tree-planting, restoring ecosystems and improving carbon in soils. Other “novel” forms of CDR are still in development. Carbon uptake methods in the oceans include enhancing the ocean’s alkalinity and the fertilisation of phytoplankton by adding iron. On land, enhanced natural processes include adding charcoal to soils (“biochar”), and accelerating the creation of carbonates from rock weathering. There are also more technological interventions. These include “bioenergy with carbon capture and storage” (Beccs), in which biomass is burned for energy and the emissions captured and stored underground; and “direct air capture”, the removal of CO₂ from the air with advanced machines. All of these methods are now being piloted, but remain expensive. Some of them also raise environmental risks: before any could be used at significant scale, countries would need to be sure that they would not have negative side-effects. In turn that means the world needs to think seriously about their governance. The politics of cooling the planet But there is currently no place for such talks. Neither novel methods of carbon dioxide removal, nor increasing the earth’s reflectivity, are formally part of the Cop negotiations or indeed any other UN policy process. This is because many countries have believed that any discussion of these would take the pressure off emissions reduction. They have been supported in this view by some of the larger climate NGOs, who have not wanted anything to distract from their campaign against fossil fuels. But the world has changed. Climate science says emissions reduction on its own can no longer keep us on a safe climate pathway. This surely makes blanket opposition to novel CDR and cooling methods untenable. Governments need to be scaling up research into these methods and considering their governance. At the very least, they should be talking about them. This is why the latest moves at Cop31 are so important. At this point it is not clear whether countries will agree to a statement on how to respond to overshoot. Some are still opposed. But if the final text does acknowledge that active cooling will be needed, it will mark the beginning of a new era in climate action. Michael Jacobs receives funding from the Climate Hub, a non-profit organisation aiming to raise awareness of the latest climate science and its implications for policy. He is a member of the Labour Party.
6922adfa77cdfe45: PONTIAN, Nov 19 — The Johor state government has ordered an immediate halt to land reclamation works at a project site suspected of using construction waste believed to have originated from a neighbouring country at Jalan Kampung Tenggayun, Mukim Rimba Terjun, here. dae6f5d8afc635c4: THE HAGUE, Nov 19 — Myanmar committed genocide against its Rohingya minority, the International Court of Justice said on Thursday in an historic ruling, ordering refugees be given safe passage home and awarded compensation. The ruling by the top UN court was the first time in its 80-year history that ICJ judges have determined that a state committed genocide, and is likely to be seen as justice for Rohingya victims of Myanmar’s brutal 2017 crackdown. “The Republic of the Union of Myanmar has committed genocide against the Rohingya group in northern Rakhine State,” said ICJ President Yuji Iwasawa, delivering the verdict in the court’s Great Hall of Justice in The Hague. For nearly three hours, Iwasawa laid out searing evidence of Myanmar’s atrocities against its mostly Muslim Rohingya minority during the campaign, which forced hundreds of thousands to flee into neighbouring Bangladesh. Myanmar’s security forces killed thousands of Rohingya civilians, committed “widespread sexual violence” against women and “extreme violence” against children, Iwasawa said. Rohingya villages were “systemically destroyed” and replaced with non-Rohingya inhabitants, said the ICJ, ruling that the “only reasonable inference” was that Myanmar intended to destroy the population—a key test for genocide. ‘Safe’ return The court ordered Myanmar to “allow and facilitate the safe, voluntary, and dignified return to their place of residence” for those who fled the violence. Judges also told Myanmar it must investigate and punish anyone suspected of committing genocide, providing for compensation to be determined at a later date. While the decisions of the ICJ are binding and cannot be appealed, the court has no way of enforcing its verdicts, and it remains to be seen whether Myanmar’s rulers will adhere to the orders. But the ruling will likely heap more international pressure on its leader Min Aung Hlaing. He commanded the military during the Rohingya crackdown before ousting the elected government of Aung San Suu Kyi in a 2021 coup. This year, he was installed as civilian president following deeply restricted elections and is waging a diplomatic campaign for legitimacy—which may be complicated by the ruling. The landmark ICJ verdict was also being closely watched by legal experts for clues into how the court will rule in another high-profile case before it—whether Israel has committed genocide in Gaza. ‘I want justice’ For the more than one million Rohingya now living in the world’s largest refugee camp over the border in Bangladesh, the ruling offered a glimmer of hope for accountability. “I want justice,” a 23-year-old Rohingya rape survivor said before the verdict in the cramped shelter where she lives with her family. “There should be stringent punishment for those who raped women. The ICJ should say something separately about this,” she said, requesting anonymity. Survivors of the violence brought with them harrowing tales of gang rapes, mass executions, and cruelty towards families and children. Far from the squalor of the refugee camps, the panel of 15 judges has been weighing for seven years whether Myanmar’s actions constitute genocide. The case was brought by The Gambia under the 1948 UN Genocide Convention, which allows any state to bring a case against another it suspects of breaching the international agreement set up after World War II. Myanmar had always denied genocide, arguing that its actions targeted a military uprising from insurgents after a series of attacks left a dozen security personnel dead. “Myanmar was not obliged to remain idle and allow terrorists to have free rein,” its representative Ko Ko Hlaing told judges during hearings on the case in January. The Gambia’s justice minister said the country filed the case “after reviewing credible reports of the most brutal and vicious violence imaginable inflicted upon a vulnerable group that had been dehumanised and persecuted for many years.” The Gambia has the “full backing and support” of the 57-member Organisation of Islamic Cooperation for its efforts at the ICJ, said the minister, Dawda Jallow. “It is not about esoteric issues of international law, it is about real people, real stories and a real group of human beings,” added Jallow. Speaking before the verdict, survivor Mohammed Osman said he was hoping the ruling would allow him to go back home and perform last rites for his parents and younger brother killed by the Myanmar military. “They shot my father dead, forced my mother into a house with a few other women, raped them and burnt down our homestead,” Osman, 20, told AFP. — AFP
24a63d0290cf3133: GEORGE TOWN, Nov 19 — The RM8.4 billion Capacity Charge payable over 40 years under the Bulk Water Supply Agreement (BWSA) between Penang and Perak represents deferred payments to recover the construction costs of a water treatment plant built specifically to supply water to Penang. Penang Chief Minister Chow Kon Yeow said the charge, amounting to RM210 million annually, was an “availability payment” for the plant’s capacity. It is a standard payment mechanism in long-term bulk water supply agreements and is separate from charges for the actual volume of water supplied, he said. He explained that the water treatment plant, with a capacity of 500 million litres per day (MLD), was constructed exclusively to supply the Penang Water Supply Corporation (PBAPP), at an estimated construction cost of RM3 billion. “When financing costs and plant renewal works over the 40 years are taken into account, the total amount comes to RM8.4 billion. This figure has undergone scrutiny and review by financial consultants appointed to conduct due diligence on the project. “Prasarana Air dan Irigasi Perak (PAIP) is responsible for securing the financing and bearing the construction risks, while PBAPP is not required to make any upfront payments or capital contributions to PAIP,” he said in a statement today. Yesterday, Bagan Member of Parliament Lim Guan Eng, who is also a former Penang Chief Minister, questioned why PBAPP was required to pay RM210 million annually for 40 years, amounting to RM8.4 billion, despite no treated water having been supplied to Penang to date. Chow, who also chairs PBA Holdings Berhad (PBAHB) and PBAPP, explained that the plant’s construction costs would be recovered through the annual Capacity Charge over 40 years, beginning when water supply commences. This arrangement, he said, would spread the financial commitment over the agreement’s duration, making the payments more manageable for PBAPP. He added that the BWSA also provides for a separate Supply Charge, amounting to RM16.2 billion of the total RM24.6 billion payable under the agreement, which represents the cost of the water itself. Addressing concerns raised by five PBAHB directors who had expressed reservations about certain aspects of the agreement, Chow said they generally acknowledged the need to secure the water supply but had raised concerns over the payment terms. These concerns included the possible invocation of the “Perak State Interest Clause” and the implications of a prolonged suspension of water supply. Chow stressed that several safeguards had been incorporated into the agreement to protect Penang’s interests, particularly those of PBAPP. He said that under the agreement, PBAPP is only required to pay the Supply Charge based on the actual volume of water received that meets the stipulated quality standards. Furthermore, PAIP is required to compensate PBAPP at an agreed rate for every cubic metre of water shortfall or supply that fails to meet the required quality standards, as verified by an independent laboratory. He said PBAPP also retained the right to terminate the agreement and claim damages if PAIP breached its contractual obligations and failed to rectify the breach within 90 days. In the event of a water supply suspension lasting more than three months, provided the disruption was not caused by PBAPP, either party would be entitled to request a renegotiation of the agreement. This could include referring the matter to their respective state governments for mediation. “Either party may terminate the agreement only if the renegotiations fail to reach an agreement after a further three-month period. “In such circumstances, PBAPP would only be required to make a one-off payment equivalent to the outstanding balance of the Capacity Charges, discounted at a rate of four per cent per annum, instead of continuing to pay RM210 million annually until 2072,” he explained. Chow emphasised that the BWSA, which provides for a balanced allocation of risks between PBAPP and PAIP, was a strategic measure to secure Penang’s long-term water supply, particularly as the state’s existing surface water resources are projected to reach full utilisation by 2030. — Bernama

c66fd6e4f18db99e: Researchers in Australia claim they’ve kept a human liver alive, on life support, outside the body for seven weeks, opening up speculative new possibilities in biomedical engineering.

The feat, whose details are pending publication, was carried out in Sydney after a team led by surgeon and inventor Carlo Pulitano connected a donated liver to a system of automated pumps and sensors that fed the organ nutrients, supplied it with blood, and whisked away waste.

In an interview, Pulitano, a transplant surgeon at the Royal Prince Alfred Hospital and a professor at the University of Sydney, likened the life support system to “an artificial body.” Its official name is the Extended Organ Perfusion System.
“Our group is the only one in the world to have maintained a human liver under fully normothermic, physiological conditions for seven weeks,” he says.

Normothermic means body temperature, or about 37 °C. The previous record for keeping an internal organ alive outside the body was set in Switzerland several years ago. That organ—also a liver—lasted around two weeks.

Most organs destined for transplant survive only a few hours in special ice buckets and need to be raced to their destination. Over the last decade, however, surgeons have been switching to perfusion systems, which pump warm or cold fluids into an organ. This can double the time it can be held before it must be transplanted.

Pulitano says the key to breaking the record was to automate the systems used to keep the organ thriving. During a meeting in Switzerland earlier this year, the Sydney team described perfusing 55 human livers, one after the other. Some were connected to a system that needed to be adjusted manually, but for those placed on the automated system—which produced the seven-week survivor—the average survival time tripled, to about four weeks.

Perfusion has already enabled doctors to restart hearts from dead people and keep them beating outside the body. Paulo Martins, a transplant doctor at the University of Oklahoma, says about half the kidneys he transplants are now perfused, even though the process can add $100,000 to the cost of a transplant.
While the research awaits formal publication, the eventual goal is what Pulitano and colleagues call “time-unlimited liver preservation.”

Scientists have already discovered possible medical benefits to keeping organs on life support longer than usual. One, they say, is that perfused organs apparently start to repair themselves and become stronger after a day or so. That’s what led a Swiss team, in 2022, to transplant a damaged liver that had been kept on perfusion for three days—the longest time any internal organ had remained outside the body before a successful transplant, says Waldemar Hoffmann, the CEO and cofounder of Apersys, a startup formed to commercialize the technology.
Pulitano says his own startup, Aeternum Life Technologies, will be helping with a planned trial in Sydney to transplant low-quality livers kept on perfusion for four days.

What’s less clear, says Hoffmann, is whether any transplant surgeon would ever want, or need, to use an organ kept alive for nearly two months. He says people in the field believe Pulitano’s record is real, but they don’t know how healthy the organ was at the end or even what so much extra time is likely to achieve. “The key question is what the purpose for a seven-week perfusion would be,” he says.

Yet that’s where things could start to get interesting, says Martins, the Oklahoma surgeon. Long-term life support could enable far-out concepts like artificial wombs, new types of organ manufacturing, and the chance to experiment directly on human organs outside the body for extended periods.

For his part, Pulitano says long-term machine perfusion could help grow new organs. In living donations, surgeons commonly take half of a person’s liver to give someone else. After about two months, both parts will have grown back almost to their full volume. Pulitano says he’s tried dividing a liver and then attaching the sections to the machine. If that works, he says, it could be a way to multiply one donor liver into several full-size organs.

“It’s important to have people thinking outside the box and pushing the limits and creating possibilities for things that, right now, sometimes we don’t even have a need for but are going to be needed in the future,” says Martins. “That’s how science moves.”

He’s not the only one who thinks so. For instance, a US company, Bexorg, has been reanimating human brains using perfusion pumps. The idea is to study what effects experimental drugs have on them. That company perfuses brains for about a day but has said it wants to extend the time to two weeks.

Similar experiments can be done on livers, says Pulitano, who has already tried adding gene therapies to the organs. “It gives us a living human organ model for translational research that no animal system can match, because the biology, the immunology, and the drug responses are human from the outset,” he says.

Meanwhile, in Silicon Valley, patents filed by Altos Labs, a billionaire-backed longevity startup, describe attempts to introduce reprogramming genes into animal livers maintained outside the body. Eventually, Altos scientists have speculated, they might temporarily disconnect a failing organ while it’s still in a person’s body, connecting it to a perfusion machine in order to douse it with ultra-powerful genetic treatments without risking the rest of the body.

Doctors probing the limits of organ life support have now formed two new scientific societies to explore the concept. One, founded by Martins and called the International Society for Organ Preservation and Perfusion Therapy, will hold its inaugural meeting this year in Italy. The other, based in China, was launched in August to advance what doctors at the First Affiliated Hospital of Sun Yat-Sen University have termed “organ medicine”: research at the level of whole organs kept alive by “bionic maintenance.”
“What is exploding is the idea of this technology that clearly goes beyond simply organ preservation,” says Pulitano. “Basically, that’s a concept that’s entirely new.”
232a74eadf93328f: LAS VEGAS, Nov 19 — Lando Norris is confident Formula 1 bosses are not putting the sport’s 2,000-strong travelling circus at risk by ending the season in West Asia, PA Media/dpa reported. Following Saturday’s race on the Las Vegas Strip, the grid’s 11 teams — 10 of which have bases in the UK – will head to Qatar for the penultimate round on November 29 before a concluding fixture in Abu Dhabi the following weekend. Imola had been placed on standby to host the final race amid the ongoing United States-Iran conflict. However, F1 chiefs confirmed last week that they will push ahead with completing the 23-round season, as planned, in West Asia. UK’s current Foreign Office advice says the situation in the region “remains deeply unpredictable and the risk of escalation is high.” It adds that “British nationals in, or planning to travel through, the Middle East should be prepared for possible flight cancellations, airspace closures, and travel disruptions,” as well as “a risk of further attacks across the region at short notice.” But speaking in Las Vegas, 27-year-old Norris, who won the previous race in Sao Paulo, said: “I am looking forward to going. From my side, I am fine. It is a big team that we travel with, and it is more, ‘what do they think?’ “But I have my friend’s wedding in Bahrain next week, so I was planning on going there anyway, and then going on to Qatar and Abu Dhabi. “So, from my side, it is not a concern. I just don’t believe that this sport would put us at risk.” The rounds in Bahrain and Saudi Arabia were cancelled earlier this year, although a ‘Bahrain Grand Prix’ was relocated to Malaysia’s Sepang venue last month. Next year’s calendar is due to begin in Bahrain and Saudi Arabia. “I don’t have any hesitation to go or know of anyone that is concerned,” said Mercedes driver George Russell ahead of the concluding two rounds. “I am sure some people have their reservations. But I know people who live in the region, and they have said it quite bluntly, that if they didn’t feel comfortable, they wouldn’t remain there with their families. “There are a lot of terrible things going on in every region of the world, and you have got to trust in the people that say it is safe. F1 are not stupid, so there is zero concern from my side. Fingers crossed it’ll all be fine.” Kimi Antonelli was crowned world champion last month in Mexico, while his Mercedes team wrapped up the constructors’ title the following weekend in Sao Paulo. Red Bull’s Max Verstappen leads the battle to finish as runner-up in the drivers’ standings. The four-time world champion is 17 points clear of Russell and 18 ahead of Lewis Hamilton ahead of Saturday’s night race. — Bernama-PA Media/dpa
4324a80b17abe87b: SHENZHEN, Nov 19 — The death of a student at a boarding school in Perak should be a reminder to all parties of the importance of shared responsibility in ensuring the well-being of children, said Prime Minister Datuk Seri Anwar Ibrahim. Anwar said he had discussed the incident with the police and Education Minister Datuk Seri Fadhlina Sidek, describing it as something he had never imagined could happen. “This is a matter that deeply troubles us. May Allah SWT protect us and remind us all — parents, friends and peers — that this is an issue we must address together as one big Malaysian family,” he told a press conference after attending the 2026 Apec Economic Leaders’ Meeting here today. As such, he called for a transparent and independent investigation rather than relying on existing departmental channels, to identify the actual cause of the incident. He added that the investigation should examine the background and factors that led to the incident, including possible family issues, peer relationships or other aspects. Anwar also questioned the supervision and care provided to students at boarding schools, particularly when students are absent from class or staying in areas such as the sick bay. “In my experience, students at boarding schools are monitored. If they do not attend class, they are usually in the sick bay. Boarding schools have designated areas for students requiring care in the sick bay. “But how come no one is assigned to look after the sick bay?” he said. However, Anwar said it was important not to disclose excessive details regarding the incident out of respect for the victim’s family, while emphasising the importance of handling the matter with sensitivity. — Bernama

6e7bffe44ecc98c1: IPOH, Nov 19 — A newborn baby girl, believed to have been stabbed by her biological mother, died in an incident in Pantai Remis on November 14. Perak police chief Datuk Mohd Alwi Zainal Abidin said the incident is believed to have occurred on the day the baby was born, at about 1pm. This incident was uncovered after the baby’s mother told one of her friends about it. “Her friend, feeling guilty, came forward to make a police report, which led to the investigation and the arrest of the victim’s mother and her boyfriend,” he said at a press conference at the Perak police contingent headquarters here today. Mohd Alwi said that the initial investigation found two stab wounds on the baby’s chest, believed to have been made with a sharp weapon. “We have obtained the weapon believed to have been used by the suspect in the incident,” he said, adding that both suspects have been remanded for six days since yesterday until Nov 23 to assist in the investigation under Section 302 of the Penal Code. He added that the teenager would be sent for a psychiatric examination to determine the condition of her mental health. — Bernama

Nadarajah (Youth, Sports and NGOs). “The other two are Rim assemblywoman Datuk Khaidhirah Abu Zahar (Women, Family and Community Development) and Bukit Katil assemblyman Muhammad Ridzuan Mohd Sarif (Agriculture, Environment and Disaster Management),” he told reporters after the ceremony here today. 6fef8c47ef555446: KUALA LUMPUR, November 19 — Forget the blue wave — Bukit Jalil is drowning in an emo wave tonight as My Chemical Romance (MCR) kicks off the first night of The Black Parade 2026 in KL. The TM National Stadium in Bukit Jalil, serving as the tour’s penultimate venue, will host the rock band on November 19 and 20 with an estimated 120,000 fans attending both days. By early this morning, fans had already begun arriving, many clad in all-black outfits, some complete with MCR-themed face makeup and face paint. The hype for MCR has been building since the KL stop was announced last year and despite the postponement that moved the original April and May dates to November, fans are still going above and beyond to welcome MCR back to Malaysia after nearly 19 years. From an MCR-themed running event and an after party to trading customised fan freebies packs, Malaysians are ready for The Black Parade 2026. Twenty-six-year-old Akmal Hady is one of the founders of a Klang Valley-based running community collective called Langgar Limit, and the group recently organised an MCR-themed running event in Petaling Jaya. “The idea for The Black Parade run came from one of our crew members, Muaz, back in July 2025 when tickets first went on sale. “Basically, it’s a short run followed by a DJ after-party at Underturntable in PJ. “We had a great turnout — around 80 people showed up,” Hady told Malay Mail. Hady added that many participants even came in their best emo-style sporting getups with some wearing band tees, chains, boots, makeup and eyeliner. “Growing up, I listened to a lot of emo music, and MCR is easily one of the biggest icons of the subculture. “After going to so many emo night gigs over the years, my team and I finally managed to organise one ourselves — and I’m honestly so proud of us,” Hady said. Meanwhile, 19-year-old Danny is one of the admins of the @fansprojectmcr_msia Instagram page and is currently on a mission to execute a fan project, a hybrid physical and digital fan light-up project in collaboration with a couple of local MCR fan pages, including @mcrxmalaysia and @MCRmymsia. The fan light-up project uses a mix of 20,000 red paper cutouts (printed with QR code instructions for the seating zones) and red-and-blue digital backgrounds that fans display on their phone screens at full brightness. They are asking participating fans to light up their phones or put up the cutouts during several songs throughout the concert. “We started planning about two weeks after tickets dropped last year for the original April date. At first, around 80 people volunteered, but after the postponement, many members backed out quite late. “Now we’re down to about 20 people, which made our original plan of printing 160,000 two-coloured papers impossible. Instead, we printed 20,000 red cutouts with QR instructions mainly for the seating zones, and switched to digital red and blue screens that fans can screenshot and display at full brightness,” Danny said. Danny was inspired to do the fan project after seeing MCR frontman Gerard Way’s reaction towards another light-up fan project at their previous concerts. He even made a new circle of online friends through Aling and Aiman over their shared love for MCR and, having never met face-to-face, the first night of the concert will mark their first real-life meetup. “Two weeks after tickets went on sale, I searched to see if any Malaysians were doing something similar (fan project) and found a post by Aling that barely had any engagement. “I reached out to her and the only person who commented on her post, Aiman, and we started a WhatsApp group to recruit more people. “What’s crazy is that we’ve never met in real life — we’ve only ever talked online, and today will be our first time meeting,” Danny said, adding that the rest of the team consists of members from various age groups, ranging from Millennials to Gen Z. While most fans have been supportive, the team has faced gatekeeping from rock purists calling the project “too K-pop” and questioning whether they are “real rockers” — criticism the team takes in stride. “The reception has been a bit of a mixed bag. “Most people are backing us and sharing our posts, but there are definitely a few calling us ‘not real rockers’ or saying we’re acting like K-pop fans. “Some people agree with that take, and honestly, we get it — you can’t please everyone,” he said. Bringing a heavy dose of early-2000s nostalgia to Bukit Jalil, 34-year-old small business owner Teh Fatimah Md Sidik — founder of custom printing brand Tehreka Studio — is handing out free retro cassette cover inserts and selling custom cassette fan packs across both nights of the concert. Inspired by fans sharing handmade crafts online and the lasting memories attached to physical music memorabilia, she wanted to create tangible keepsakes that would remind concertgoers of the night they finally saw MCR live after nearly 19 years. “I started this project on Saturday, November 14, with around RM70 in capital for 200 freebie packs. “I handled everything myself, from designing and mock-ups to printing, cutting, and packaging and it’s been completely worth it. “Beyond introducing Tehreka Studio, I didn’t expect so many people to love the cassette concept because it brings back their teenage memories,” Teh told Malay Mail. There is no shortage of fans dressing up in their gothic and emo outfits in Bukit Jalil today, and one of them is 31-year-old Nur Fatin Shafiqa Mohd Norman from Batu Pahat, Johor. Shafiqa came clad in a black jacket, a handmade red songket tailored by her mother just a couple of days earlier, along with a black veil adorned with a black rose and gothic-themed makeup. “We arrived in KL from Johor yesterday and we stayed at a hostel in KL and will be heading back to Batu Pahat tonight after the concert. “We arrived at the stadium around 9am this morning because we were afraid that the parking would be full here. She also revealed that she had to wake up at around 4.45am this morning to start dressing up for the concert. It took her around two hours to finish her look today. “I’ve been listening to MCR since my school days. “Even though the postponement dampened the hype for a bit, the excitement definitely came rushing back as the new date got closer,” she said. Tonight marks the first night of MCR’s The Black Parade 2026 in KL. The concert opened with a performance by local rap-rock group Pop Shuvit at 7.15pm before MCR takes the stage at 8.30pm.

11c1f6c108023853: Over the past week, anyone could be forgiven for wondering whether a Diehard IV–style cyberwar had finally arrived in the US.

Across just four consecutive business days, a mass Microsoft exchange outage broke IT services for thousands of companies, a Federal Aviation Administration tech screw-up grounded airplanes across the country, a software problem affecting JPMorgan Chase caused another round of disruption, a United Airlines system glitch delayed flights yet again, and an NSA classified network’s downtime left the agency’s staff sitting at home waiting to return to their office at Fort Meade. In the midst of a US war with Iran and rising fears of AI-enabled hacking, this still-unfolding comedy of IT errors colliding across American infrastructure felt to plenty of observers like more than a coincidence.

Yet there’s still no evidence that any one of these clustered technological failures were related, much less caused by hackers. Their improbable, sequential timing left Americans anxiously doomscrolling for signs of foul play. But in cases like these, it’s the job of cybersecurity analysts (and reporters at WIRED) to determine—vibes aside—whether the latest tech outage was actually an accident or the result of a cyberattack.

3d858e2a650679b4: After a tough few years littered with some high-profile failures, there’s some positive news for next-generation batteries in the US.

Sila just signed an agreement with Panasonic Energy, a global battery manufacturer, to supply silicon-carbon anode material, a possible key to smaller, lighter batteries. It’s a deal that Sila says could be worth more than $1 billion over time.

This arrangement also shows how much the politics of batteries have shifted lately. A major part of the financial backing for this factory’s production is a $1.4 billion loan from the Trump administration’s Defense Department. While batteries can be a major tool to help drive the energy transition and cut emissions, right now much of the industry is more focused on geopolitics.

Founded in 2011, Sila makes silicon-based anodes for lithium-ion batteries. The big selling point here is the potential to improve energy density—Sila’s anode weighs a fifth as much as the graphite used in anodes today and cuts the volume in half, according to the company. So using this new material enables batteries to pack more energy into the same weight and volume, allowing longer range for EVs, for example. The material can also deliver more power and recharge faster, compared with conventional chemistry.
We’ve been following Sila (and its competitors) for years. My colleague James Temple covered the company when its battery first appeared in Whoop fitness wearables in 2021.

Things have gotten a lot bigger since then. In 2022, Sila announced plans for a factory in Moses Lake, Washington, and received $100 million from the US Department of Energy, part of a multibillion-dollar round of grants under the Biden administration to support the US battery supply chain.

The company opened its factory in September 2025, and it’s already operating. But the deal with Panasonic will help it scale to at least 10 times more production than current levels, says Gene Berdichevsky, the company’s cofounder and CEO.
Panasonic has committed to buying tens of thousands of tons of material, Berdichevsky says, though Sila isn’t sharing specific numbers on the total commitment or the price Panasonic is paying.

This agreement is Sila’s first mass-market deal and a big one for the United States’ next-generation battery market, which has largely been on the ropes over the past few years. Two billion-dollar battery companies, 24M and ESS Tech, have declared bankruptcy and shut down just in the last year.

The glimmer of hope here is tied up with something I’ve been noticing about this industry: the shifting politics. While batteries used to be firmly considered a climate technology, we’ve seen a lot of companies move away from messaging around the clean energy transition and lean into geopolitics.

China dominates the battery world and particularly the battery anode market, controlling over 90% of graphite production today. For years, the US has been trying to curb reliance on Chinese batteries, battery materials, and other materials used in crucial technologies, like rare earth metals. But the Trump administration has ramped things up, and earlier this year the US Defense Department committed a $1.4 billion loan to Sila aimed at helping the US face a “significant technology sovereignty challenge,” as a press release put it.

Sila’s announcement of the Panasonic deal does mention EVs—but not climate, emissions or the energy transition. Rather, it’s all about American industrialization. (And, of course, a mention that a North American battery supply chain can also help power the AI market.)
I asked Berdichevsky about this shift and whether the company holds decarbonization as a priority.

“I think the politics of it has shifted around us much more than our motivations have shifted,” he said. “It’s really the energy efficiency that motivates engineers like myself and technologists at our company. And I still think that that’s still at the heart of it.”
This article is from The Spark, MIT Technology Review’s weekly climate newsletter. To receive it in your inbox every Wednesday, sign up here.

74fbfcd64d12556a: In the Guria region, an organization is helping people recover a history the Soviets tried to erase
Originally published on Global Voices
Resort in the Guria region of Georgia. Photo by Tinari.totoro on Wikimedia Commons (CC BY-SA 4.0).

This interview is part of a series of spotlights on the work of some of the grantees of the Digital Spark granting scheme, as part of the Regional Support Mechanism EECA project, implemented by the Metamorphosis Foundation and TechSoup, in partnership with CIVICUS and under the Digital Democracy Initiative (DDI) that covers the Global South. It is being published on Global Voices as part of a content-sharing agreement.

Guria is a region in Georgia, situated in the southwestern part of the country. It has a coastline on the Black Sea to the west, which is about 22 kilometers (13 miles) long, and the region is bordered by the Samegrelo-Zemo Svaneti region to the north, Imereti to the east, and the Autonomous Republic of Adjara to the south. It has a rich history and a historical tradition of democracy.
Today, in the region, independent media access is limited and digital literacy remains low. However, Guria has a civic tradition that most of its own residents do not know about in detail.

In 1904, locals organized protests against imperial (Russian, at the time) institutions, formed institutions of self-governance, and proclaimed the Gurian Republic, an early experiment in participatory democracy.

The republic was violently suppressed first by the Russian tsarist empire, and later all the memories of it were fragmented further by decades of deliberate erasure under Soviet occupation of Georgia (1921–1991) and by repressions.
This is exactly what the Digital Spark Spotlight project in Georgia focused on: history and memory in the Guria region.
Global Voices interviewed Lika Mergaladze, head of the organization Komli Initiative for Civic Engagement, about their project: what they have done and what they learned through it.
Global Voices (GV): Please tell us about your organization and why you chose to get involved with the Digital Spark project?

Lika Mergaladze (LM): Our organization, Komli Initiative for Civic Engagement, works to preserve local history, strengthen civic engagement, and promote sustainable development in the Guria region of Georgia. We use exhibitions, workshops, digital storytelling, and collaborative activities to connect communities with their history and encourage active participation in civic life.

We chose to get involved in the Digital Spark project because we saw an opportunity to combine local history with modern digital technologies. We wanted to help community members document and share their family stories, develop digital skills, and better understand the connection between the past and present. We believe that preserving historical memory and encouraging critical thinking are essential for building an informed and active community.
GV: What issue/challenge in your community prompted you to undertake this project?

LM: One of the main challenges in Guria is that many important historical stories have been forgotten or remain untold. These stories were purposely erased during the Soviet Union. Many families who were the victims of a series of repressions in the 1920s and 30s learned to remain silent about their past in the 50s after World War II. As a result, younger generations often know very little about their ancestors and the region’s democratic traditions, including the Gurian Republic of 1904.

Another challenge is limited access to independent media and low levels of digital literacy in local communities. The dominance of social media and television as information sources makes media literacy and critical thinking particularly important.

We undertook this project to address these challenges by helping local people preserve their history, recognize misinformation and propaganda, and use digital tools to share their stories with a wider audience.
GV: What are the key changes/activities that your organization implemented during your participation in the project?

LM: Through the project ‘From Understanding the Past to the Digital Future,’ implemented from April to October 2026, we organized several activities across the three municipalities of Guria: Ozurgeti, Chokhatauri, and Lanchkhuti. Our main activities included a public discussion. On June 24, we organized ‘What Drove Gurians Crazy? Propaganda Now and Then,’ exploring Guria’s democratic history, Soviet occupation, propaganda, and contemporary challenges. We also did digital storytelling workshops, an AI and Digital Creation workshop and a theatrical performance: on August 12, we presented “My Days and My Father’s Diaries,” dedicated to Meri Chanukvadze and her father, Amberki Chanukvadze, whose life reflected the impact of Soviet repression. These activities helped strengthen participants’ digital skills, encourage historical research, and create opportunities for community members to share their stories online.
GV: How did your participation in the project impact your organization’s beneficiaries and the community that you serve? Please provide examples.

LM: The project generated strong interest across all three municipalities, reaching nearly 50 community members, with particularly strong participation from women and young people. Locals participated in the digital storytelling workshop, including 12 women. These activities gave participants practical opportunities to develop their digital skills and explore new ways of communicating important ideas. Another meaningful example was the theatrical performance dedicated to Meri and her father. More than 35 people attended and participated in a discussion afterwards. The performance encouraged people to reflect on the experiences of families affected by Soviet repression and the importance of preserving historical memory.

The project also laid the foundation for a cross-municipal network of young people, activists, and aspiring digital storytellers. This network can help community members continue documenting local history, sharing civic information, and engaging in public discussions beyond the project itself.
GV: How has your own knowledge, awareness, and experience with digital democracy and civic space changed, thanks to your participation in the project?

LM: Our participation in the project strengthened our understanding of how digital technologies can support civic engagement and democratic participation. We gained greater awareness of the importance of digital storytelling, media literacy, and critical thinking in helping communities understand their history and respond to contemporary challenges. We also explored how AI-assisted content creation can provide new opportunities for preserving local stories and making them accessible to wider audiences. The project reinforced our belief that digital tools are not simply communication technologies; they can also help people participate in public life, challenge misinformation, and contribute to community development. Most importantly, we recognized that connecting historical memory with modern digital tools can help create a more informed, active, and engaged society.
GV: What are the most valuable lessons and experiences you are taking away from this project?

LM: One of the most valuable lessons was that many people are interested in learning about their history when they are given a welcoming space to ask questions and share experiences. Family stories can open up broader conversations about democracy, human rights, repression, and civic responsibility.

We also learned that practical workshops and collaborative activities are effective ways to introduce digital tools to community members. The strong participation of women and young people demonstrated the potential for inclusive, community-based learning.

Another important lesson was the value of combining traditional storytelling with digital technologies. Personal stories, family diaries, public discussions, and theatrical performances can make historical events more relatable and meaningful.
GV: What comes next? How will you apply the learning and digital capacity you have built in your future work and within your community?
LM: We plan to build on the experience and connections developed through the project by continuing to document, digitize, and share historical and civic stories from Guria.

We aim to encourage more community members, especially young people and women, to use digital storytelling and online content creation to preserve family histories and discuss local issues. We also intend to apply the knowledge gained from the workshops to future educational activities, community discussions, and collaborative initiatives.

An important priority will be to strengthen the network of local journalists, activists, and digital storytellers across Ozurgeti, Chokhatauri, and Lanchkhuti. By supporting collaboration and knowledge-sharing, we hope to ensure that these activities continue beyond the project period.
Written by Daria Dergacheva
c9e737dd8e066bae: HONG KONG, Nov 19 — Tech firms mostly rose today following a record IPO from Claude-creator Anthropic, but trading was cautious as investors deal with the fallout from the crisis engulfing AI titan Nvidia. Expectations that the Federal Reserve will continue to hike interest rates into the new year also weighed on sentiment as policymakers struggle to bring down inflation, even after a recent drop in oil prices. In a highly anticipated initial public offering, Anthropic priced its shares at US$83 (RM341) each, raising more than US$80 billion, which could rise to more than US$100 billion — topping SpaceX’s blockbuster sale in June. The pricing values the firm at around US$1.5 trillion, making it one of the biggest on the planet. The firm will debut later Thursday. The news reinforced confidence in the AI sector, which has been hammered this week by the resignation of Nvidia boss Jensen Huang over extramarital affairs with several women, including one suspected of being a Chinese spy. “Anthropic’s IPO is a big near-term win for the tech sector and should help restore some investor confidence that the AI Revolution growth thesis is not waning,” Dan Ives of Yorkville Ives & Co said in a note, adding that Nvidia’s troubles had cast a shadow over the sector. Nvidia’s scandal has compounded growing concerns about the eye-watering sums pumped into the artificial intelligence buildout and when that would see a profit, if at all. Traders have also been spooked by the US Commerce Department’s move to close a loophole allowing Chinese companies to access Nvidia’s powerful AI chips remotely, adding to worries that a new Democratic-led Congress would impose new regulations. Futures in Wall Street’s three main indexes spiked on the Anthropic news, with the Nasdaq’s up around one per cent. But Asian traders were a little more cautious. 19d132bfd53eb32c: From MyPower Corporation

As delegates gathered in Vienna, Austria, for the 70th International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA) general conference, geopolitical tensions continued to show how events thousands of kilometres away can disrupt energy markets, supply chains and fuel prices.
These are very different challenges, but they remind us of something Malaysia cannot take for granted: resilience and energy security.
How do we ensure that our electricity system remains reliable, secure and cost-competitive as demand grows, while also moving towards cleaner energy?
There is no simple answer, and no single technology can meet every need. Nuclear energy is one of the options Malaysia is examining, and this is not our first time doing so.

Malaysia joined the IAEA on Jan 15, 1969 as its 101st member. Over five decades later, the agency has grown to more than 180 member states, reflecting the expanding role of nuclear science and technology around the world.

For Malaysia, nuclear technology has never been solely about electricity generation. Nuclear science at the domestic scene is always about supporting peaceful applications in areas such as medicine, agriculture, industry, research and environmental monitoring.

We have explored nuclear power before. Earlier efforts included feasibility studies and the establishment of the Malaysia Nuclear Power Corporation (MNPC) in 2011 as the country's nuclear energy programme implementing organisation. That programme did not ultimately proceed as planned.
Today's assessment therefore does not mean Malaysia is starting from zero. Neither is it simply reviving an earlier project. We are revisiting the nuclear question, but in a very different world.

In tandem with the nation's economic growth, electricity demand is also growing. Data centres and new industries are intensely changing the shape of future demand growth. As Malaysia moves towards a cleaner energy system, energy security has become increasingly important amid geopolitical uncertainty.

Malaysia is not alone in taking time to consider nuclear power. Bangladesh first explored the Rooppur project in the 1960s, but construction only began decades later in 2017. Turkey also made several attempts before the construction of its first nuclear power plant at Akkuyu began in 2018. Many other countries have also taken long journeys towards nuclear power.

Closer to home, Vietnam has revived its nuclear power development plan and has requested an IAEA Phase 2 Integrated Nuclear Infrastructure Review mission, while the Philippines is also moving forward with preparations for a nuclear power programme.
Their experiences show that the path to nuclear power is rarely straightforward. Countries may pause, reassess and adjust plans as national priorities and circumstances change.

Their experiences do not mean Malaysia should follow the same path. Every country has its circumstances. They simply remind us that nuclear programmes rarely move in a straight line. Governments change, economies progress, technology develops and national priorities evolve.

That was the broader context for Malaysia's participation in the IAEA conference from Sept 14 to 18. The scale of the gathering is significant. The IAEA brings together more than 180 member states, and 36 ministers attended this year's conference alongside senior officials, regulators, scientists and representatives of international organisations.

Malaysia's delegation was headed by the energy transition and water transformation ministry (Petra) secretary-general, with representatives from the Malaysian permanent mission in Vienna, Malaysian Nuclear Agency, atomic energy department and MyPower Corporation.

Malaysia delivered its national statement, sharing the country's progress in the peaceful uses of nuclear science and technology, and the work under way to assess the possible role of nuclear energy in electricity generation.

Malaysia has also been elected to serve on the IAEA governors board for 2026-2028, giving it a greater role in the agency's governance and discussions on nuclear safety, security, safeguards, peaceful uses and international cooperation.
The general conference, bilateral meetings and side events provide a platform for countries to exchange experiences across the much wider world of nuclear science and technology.

A key highlight of Malaysia's engagement in Vienna was the bilateral meeting with IAEA director-general Rafael Mariano Grossi, which reaffirmed the importance of international cooperation in strengthening national nuclear infrastructure.
Malaysia shared its ongoing preparations and plans for an Integrated INIR Phase 1 mission to independently assess progress and identify areas for improvement.

For Malaysia, the priority is not deciding when to build a nuclear power plant, but ensuring that the country has the knowledge, institutions and capabilities to make an informed decision. Malaysia remains in Phase 1 of the IAEA milestones approach, with no firm decision yet on nuclear power deployment, technology, vendor or site.

Malaysians will understandably have questions. Is nuclear safe? How much will it cost? What happens to radioactive waste? Who pays for the plant and its eventual decommissioning? Are our institutions ready?
These are fair questions. They deserve clear answers. Studying nuclear does not mean advocating for it. Equally, we should not dismiss an option before understanding what it can, and cannot, offer.

Renewable energy will remain central to Malaysia's energy transition. But our challenge is broader than adding renewable capacity. We must also consider what the electricity system will need as demand grows and the role of coal declines.

The haze during the week of the conference was a visible reminder of our environmental challenges. Geopolitical uncertainty offers another reminder that energy security and resilience matter, too. There is no single technology that solves every problem.
Malaysia's presence in Vienna should therefore not be read as a signal that we have already chosen nuclear power. It means we are preparing to make an informed choice.
The IAEA can provide expertise, international experience and independent peer review. Countries that have travelled on this road can tell us what worked and, just as importantly, what did not.

Ultimately, the decision belongs to Malaysia. Our task today is not to rush towards a reactor but to ask difficult questions, develop our people, strengthen our institutions and understand the responsibilities involved.
For something that could shape Malaysia's energy system for generations, doing the homework first is not a delay. It is simply a pertinent process and a responsible action.
MyPower Corporation is the government agency coordinating electricity sector reforms and nuclear power planning.

82784f45b9bc8eaa: PARIS, Nov 19 — The crisis in the Middle East sparked in February by the US and Israeli bombing of Iran has created the “largest threat” to energy security in history, the International Energy Agency (IEA) warned today. The agency said in its flagship annual World Energy Outlook that consumers were increasingly footing the bill as the world runs out of ways to absorb the impact of the conflict on energy supplies. The crisis, just like previous energy shocks, would certainly leave “lasting marks”, the agency warned. Gulf countries have been struggling to export oil since Iran began blockading the Strait of Hormuz and targeting tankers in the area, following US and Israeli strikes that sparked the crisis in February. Despite attempts by the United States to escort vessels through the channel — which pre-crisis carried about one-fifth of global oil shipments — supply lines remain severely disrupted. “The Strait of Hormuz crisis has created the largest threat to energy security in history, one that dwarfs the scale of the oil shocks of the 1970s,” IEA Executive Director Fatih Birol wrote in his foreword to the report. He highlighted the efforts countries had taken to protect households, with producing nations bringing more supplies into the market and using alternative routes, and China buying less from international markets. “Governments have intervened to try and provide some shelter for consumers, but they have nonetheless faced higher prices and, in some cases, shortfalls of supply,” Birol wrote. The report said elsewhere that “increasingly it is falling to consumers — and high prices — to absorb the impact as other buffers are run down”. Birol had struck a more hopeful tone in July when he wrote that the oil market was still benefiting from “several cushioning factors”. ‘No pathway’ back The IEA’s report comes as nations meet for the COP31 climate talks in Turkey, with governments under pressure to tackle climate change after a year of searing heatwaves and wildfires in Europe, and deadly floods in Nepal. The agency uses three scenarios for its energy outlook: a cautious one takes into account policies that are currently in place, a middle scenario looks at “stated” government policies including measures that have yet to be adopted, and a third considers a world that reaches net zero emissions by 2050. In its middle scenario, the IEA forecasts that global oil demand will reach a peak around 2030 before a slow decline, while gas demand would increase until around 2035. For this report, it also adds two other scenarios based on what might happen if the Middle East crisis persists. “While the energy sector and the global economy have shown considerable resilience, the longer the crisis lasts, the deeper the effects will be,” Birol said in a press release. “And I don’t see any credible pathway for the energy world to return to the way it was before.” — AFP

fd4601690c0a7216: PETALING JAYA, Nov 19 — Putrajaya has several ways to safeguard Malaysia’s dual 5G model beyond its golden share in Digital Nasional Bhd (DNB), including legislation and conditions attached to spectrum assignments, says an industry expert. Jake Saunders, vice-president for Asia at technology intelligence firm ABI Research, said the government’s golden share already provides one safeguard. “The Malaysian government does have its Golden Share in DNB, which gives the Malaysian government a vital say in the future endeavours of DNB,” he said. However, Saunders said different policy instruments offered different strengths if Putrajaya wanted to preserve Malaysia’s access to separate technology ecosystems over the longer term. “It is a complex topic. Legislation is a very durable solution; ministerial direction is always beneficial and can help direct and galvanise government agencies,” he said. “Going further, setting out spectrum conditions/ assignments can be more hardcoded. That is, set rights of access and/or limitations on transfers that can also applied for a guaranteed duration of time.” Saunders said maintaining access to a wide range of technologies was important as geopolitical developments, mergers and acquisitions could gradually narrow the options available to countries. “Throughout history, technology innovation has always accelerated in the most open and most diverse markets, and yet mergers & acquisition as well as geo-politics over time can inevitability constrain options.” He said Malaysia was well placed to benefit from technologies emerging from both China and Western-aligned economies. “Malaysia has always been at the crossroads of Asia and the rest of the world, and it would be prudent that the widest possible access to technologies — such as chipsets, smart devices, infrastructure hardware, for data centres, cellular networks, AI R&D and implementation — is kept open,” he added. “Offering a dual technology stack, or lane, would ensure DNB and indeed the wider Malaysian economy has competitive access to all technologies, the wider technology ecosystem and its opportunities.” DNB currently operates one of Malaysia’s two wholesale 5G networks, while U Mobile has been selected to operate the second network. DNB’s network was built by Ericsson, while U Mobile is being supported by Huawei and ZTE. The government is also transferring ownership of DNB to CelcomDigi, Maxis and YTL, although Putrajaya retains its golden share. Switching technologies not straightforward Saunders said DNB could technically change parts of its network technology over time, but replacing an established 5G system would involve more than simply changing equipment. In 2021, Ericsson signed a 10-year contract with DNB that covers an end-to-end network encompassing the core network, radio access network, transport systems, operations and business support systems, and managed services. Saunders said there was greater flexibility in the radio access network, where base stations and antennas could be replaced, although even this was not straightforward. “RAN base-stations and antennas could be swapped out but there would still need to be additional network planning, equipment testing, debugging and integration.” He said Ericsson also supported DNB’s operations layer through a dedicated network operations centre covering functions such as billing, faults, network performance and security. A complete replacement would therefore carry additional costs and operational complications. “A full-on swap out would certainly incur additional capital expenditure, ongoing integration costs, and longer-term debugging and network performance testing.” Saunders said there were also legal and financial considerations, including vendor financing, compliance with contractual milestones and support arrangements. He said DNB could nevertheless change its technology gradually rather than through a single wholesale replacement. Separately, Saunders said DNB would need to continue innovating following the handover, particularly as Malaysia develops its industrial automation and artificial intelligence capabilities. He said future upgrades could include newer radios at base stations in high-traffic urban areas, RedCap technology to support lower-cost devices and industrial internet-of-things applications, and greater use of available spectrum to increase capacity.

e5d8c3d4efd94fea: Burak Kara/GettyThis week, it was revealed that 100 corporations and industry groups tied to fossil fuel interests – including the US multinational ExxonMobil and French energy company TotalEnergies – have sent delegations to this year’s global climate summit COP31 in Turkey. These climate talks have a long history of lobbyist interference. More than 1,600 fossil fuel lobbyists attended the COP30 talks in Brazil last year, and more than 1,700 at the 2024 talks in Azerbaijan. This is a problem. The whole point of these long-running United Nations negotiations is to address human-caused climate change, which is primarily driven by burning oil, gas and coal – the very products these lobbyists are paid to promote. At COP31, fossil lobbyists will have been hard at work promoting fossil fuels. Their methods often draw on what academics call “discourses of delay”. This is how it works. To slow the shift away from fossil fuels, lobbyists spread disinformation, such as claiming fossil fuels are part of the solution (“gas is a transition fuel”), that future technologies will save us (carbon capture), or we’re doomed and it’s too late to act. Oil and gas companies have dramatically increased their Google ads in the month leading up to COP31, for example. Researchers have shown fossil fuel lobbyists use a two-pronged strategy. First, they point to a lack of international action as a reason for not acting on climate change at home. Second, they work to stymie progress at the same international talks. A new UN report says it’s now too late to hold the global temperature rise to 1.5°C. The world will likely pass this threshold in 2030. A big reason for this is obstruction by lobbyists of climate policies that target the root cause of climate change – fossil fuels. So, why are fossil fuel lobbyists allowed into these talks? Pushback in Brazil At last year’s COP30 summit, host country Brazil tried to push back against fossil fuel lobbyists. Alongside the UN and UNESCO, Brazil launched an international partnership to counter climate change disinformation and misinformation. Thirty countries have since signed onto the declaration, which calls out the: growing impact of disinformation, misinformation, denialism […] and other tactics used to undermine the integrity of information on climate change, which diminish public understanding, delay urgent action, and threaten the global climate response and societal stability. Lobbyists gain access to the talks in different ways, including through affiliations with non-governmental organisations and industry groups and as part of official government delegations. While this year’s draft negotiating text makes reference to information integrity, there’s still no clear code of conduct or meaningful disclosure of fossil fuel industry ties for the thousands of delegates attending COP31. There are no clear, explicit rules against spreading climate disinformation. COP30 President Andre Correa do Lago (centre) listens to his advisers at the conference in Brazil last year. Brazil has since produced a global roadmap for transitioning away from fossil fuels. Pablo Porciuncula/Getty A long history of lobbying Sadly, this story is all too familiar. For as long as there have been international climate talks, fossil fuel lobbyists have tried to persuade countries not to act with the urgency the science demands. It took more than a quarter of a century of climate talks before fossil fuels were explicitly addressed at the Glasgow COP in 2021. Until then, the focus was on greenhouse gas emissions – but not the fossil fuels causing them. Corporate fossil fuel lobbyists have been assisted by so-called petrostates, such as Russia and Saudi Arabia, whose economies are highly dependent on oil and gas production. And when the oil- and gas-producing states Azerbaijan and the United Arab Emirates hosted the COP talks in 2023 and 2024, respectively, both countries used the summit to push new fossil fuel deals. What are lobbyists targeting this time? There are more than 100 different agenda items up for debate at COP31, many of which are opposed by fossil fuel lobbyists. Negotiators are still discussing a UN initiative designed to rapidly increase efforts to cut greenhouse gas emissions, for instance. Alongside the official agenda, COP President and Turkish Environment Minister Murat Kurum released a separate “action” agenda organised around ten themes. Some of these, such as transitioning to clean energy, threaten fossil fuel interests. Fossil fuel lobbyists will likely try to block calls for phasing out coal, gas and oil – just as they did last year, where Brazil’s efforts to formalise a roadmap transitioning away from fossil fuels ran aground. Another concern for fossil fuel interests is the electrification goal, aimed at boosting electricity’s global share of final energy demand to 35% by 2035. If this translates to more electric vehicles, batteries and heat pumps in homes and electric furnaces in factories, it would mean less demand for oil and gas. That would affect profits for companies such as ExxonMobil and Shell. Australia on the tightrope Australian Climate Change Minister Chris Bowen is acting as president of negotiations at COP31 as part of a co-hosting arrangement with Turkey (also known as Turkiye). This represents a tightrope walk for Australia. Domestically, the Albanese Labor government is attempting to speed up the energy transition. Policies such as subsidising home batteries have proven a strong success. More than 600,000 households have installed batteries since the program began last year. Electric vehicle uptake is rapidly accelerating. Internationally, however, Australia remains one of the world’s largest coal and gas exporters. State and federal governments keep approving new projects. Given this, many countries have questioned Australia’s climate credibility, especially its Pacific neighbours. Prime Minister Anthony Albanese was heavily criticised for failing to mention fossil fuels in his opening COP31 speech. Just minutes before Albanese spoke, UN Secretary-General António Guterres urged countries to make fossil fuels “go the way of the dinosaurs”. “The dinosaurs did not have a lobby. Fossil fuels do,” he said. Can progress be made despite lobbyists? As COP31 enters its final days, the eyes of the world will be on Australia and Turkey. Should the co-hosts fail to get agreement on concrete steps to advance Brazil’s latest efforts to transition away from fossil fuels, many countries will be left disappointed. But despite the best efforts of the fossil fuel industry, momentum for a shift away from oil, gas and coal is gathering pace outside the UN talks. In April, nations attended the first international conference on transitioning away from fossil fuels, while the Fossil Fuel Non-Proliferation Treaty Initiative continues to gain members. As always, though, much more needs to be done, and quickly. Clamping down on lobbyists and climate misinformation is well overdue. Christian Downie receives funding from the Australian Research Council. William Kakenmaster receives funding from the Australian Research Council.

Pemilihan Yamtuan Besar Negeri Sembilan mendatang akan dipilih oleh Undang yang sah hari ini daripada Putera Empat.

24abcf689c6b9b5d: From Terence Netto
Former Sarawak DAP vice-chairman Wong King Wei has advised DAP to stay out of the Dec 12 Sarawak polls, citing the need for DAP to be friendly with the idea of state autonomy for Sarawakian parties.
Sarawakians want to assert the interests of their state after years of deferring to federal interests.
Decades-old reticence about their interests has in recent years been replaced by an assertiveness that Putrajaya cannot but respect.
The intensive battle between competing political coalitions in the peninsula makes the courtship of Sarawakian (and Sabahan) political parties imperative.
These days, the keys to Putrajaya, for peninsula aspirants, lie between Kuching and Kota Kinabalu.

Since the major Sarawakian parties have banded together into a fairly cohesive force in Gabungan Parti Sarawak (GPS), it does not make sense for DAP to be at cross-purposes with GPS components in the upcoming state polls.
As a single party, DAP may well emerge with the highest or second highest number of parliamentary seats in the next general election (GE16), which is due by February 2028.
No single party or coalition is expected to gain a simple majority in GE16.
This will require one or the other coalition in the peninsula to importune GPS to back them for the right to form the federal government.

DAP, as the anticipated holder of a sizeable number of seats in the peninsula, will be critical to negotiations with GPS, which is expected to sweep not only the state seats in the Dec 12 polls but also the parliamentary ones in GE16.
After seeing how the peninsula Malay vote is solidifying behind Umno and PAS-led Perikatan Nasional, DAP must think strategically about GE16.

Based on their performance in the Johor, Negeri Sembilan and Melaka polls, DAP's Pakatan Harapan (PH) allies PKR and Amanah are struggling to make a dent in the Malay vote, and are no more confident of the non-Malay vote bank.
Fear of the evolving collaboration between Umno and PAS will keep the Chinese vote with DAP despite discomfort with DAP’s overly compliant attitude towards Anwar Ibrahim.

DAP secretary-general Loke Siew Fook, presently unencumbered by ministerial duties, will have more time to espouse the reforms championed by PH that have been neglected by Anwar's puzzling pussyfooting.
The path is open to a de facto premiership by Loke – by careful rhetoric and subtle gesture – given Anwar's continued tepidity in pursuing the reformasi agenda.
Nuanced rhetoric and statesmanlike gestures by Loke can restrain Sarawak DAP leader Chong Chieng Jen from remonstrating against a DAP decision to refrain from contesting in the Sarawak polls.

DAP should also signal to Rafizi Ramli’s Bersama to be realistic about its chances in GE16, which will require the PKR splinter to go only for the parliamentary seats – 10 at the most – that the Rafizi claque in PKR can win in GE16.
After two underwhelming outings in Johor and Melaka, Bersama ought to come down from the clouds and see that there is no point in overrating its chances.

So, it’s a rearguard action that DAP must undertake, running into GE16, to save what can be salvaged from the growing wreck of Anwar's myopia and Amanah’s failure to convince the Malays that moderate Islam is not a delusion but a viable proposition.
It’s the high road that beckons DAP which also happens to be the pragmatic road to take in the circumstances.
Terence Netto is a senior journalist and an FMT reader.

2baef697661cb837: Dari kemelut tidak ada exco dan tak boleh buka persidangan Adun, membawa pula kepada kekalutan nama calon menteri besar baharu dikemuka kepada Yang Dipertuan Besar ketika menteri besar masih bertugas.

57de9e1d8f19559c: What began as a political impasse over the absence of a state executive council and the inability to convene the state assembly has descended into further chaos, with a new candidate for menteri besar proposed to the Yang Dipertuan Besar while the incumbent remains in office.

It is understood that during their meeting two days ago, Tuanku Muhriz Tuanku Munawir allowed Ismail Lasim to continue serving as menteri besar. So why is Umno proposing another candidate for the ruler's consideration? Could Negeri Sembilan end up with two menteris besar?
So, what happens next in Negeri Sembilan?

Ismail and Umno president Ahmad Zahid Hamidi have both expressed their desire to resolve this crisis, regardless of who instigated it, so that the state government can administer sans the unnecessary drama.
Now, I fully support what appears to be the sincerity of these two Malay leaders.
As I understand it, Ismail took the first step towards breaking the deadlock by withdrawing a letter seeking to remove Tuanku Muhriz as the state's ruler.
Ismail requested an audience with the ruler – said to be granted for Friday morning – while the 10 state executive councillors withdrew their court action and were ordered to pay legal costs.
The epilogue to this convoluted saga was fast approaching, and the public was prepared to move on to a new chapter.
But, alas, came an unexpected twist in this drama.
Umno announced that Ismail had resigned.
I initially assumed the resignation intended to reset relations between the politicians and the constitutional ruler, starting with the menteri besar's departure.
It sounded like a reasonable move. After all, Ismail and the 10 executive councillors had done plenty to incur the ruler's displeasure, which even I found unforgivable.
So it seemed encouraging that Umno wanted to put the past behind it and start afresh.

However, the Negeri Sembilan palace has yet to verify the Juasseh assemblyman's resignation as menteri besar. The comptroller of the Negeri Sembilan royal household said the supposed letter was sent only by an individual named Hamidi, who claimed to be from a law firm.
Under the state’s constitution, the menteri besar must submit his resignation to the Yang Dipertuan Besar of Negeri Sembilan, and it only takes effect with the ruler’s consent.
The palace's desire to verify the letter's authenticity certainly raises questions about it. At that point, Ismail seemed unsure which script he was supposed to follow.

Ismail's son spoke out, questioning the authenticity of the resignation letter and earning a rebuke from Zahid, who asked why family members were wading into the matter when it was an administrative issue.
Zahid has a point, but the letter itself remains perplexing.
And just as the public was trying to make sense of these conflicting scenarios, another unexpected development unfolded.
Tuanku Muhriz summoned Ismail for an audience ahead of schedule. Their meeting lasted an hour and a half.

We thought Ismail, who entered the palace as menteri besar, would emerge as an ordinary assemblyman, as Umno had announced. Instead, he walked out of the palace still holding the post of menteri besar!
So much for the audience with the ruler being the finale to this drama.
But Zahid remains adamant that only one name was submitted to Tuanku Muhriz for approval as the new menteri besar, even though Ismail is still carrying out his duties as instructed by the ruler.

For much of my life, I thought Anwar Ibrahim's imprisonment and black eye were part of the most unforgettable political saga I had ever witnessed. But I must admit, this drama is quite something, too.
What initially appeared to be a confrontation between Umno and the palace has turned into a power struggle within Umno itself.
Why is Zahid determined to replace Ismail, who now has the palace's consent to remain in office?

If Umno's top leadership wants to write another script, perhaps it should put it on hold for a year or two. Give the people of Negeri Sembilan some breathing space. This soap opera with its endless twists and turns has left us winded – though for the people's sake, I hope this saga finds some closure.
